## THE AUTHOR TO THE READER.

*The Author is in harmony with the theme he has undertaken:* <note>original Latin: "A Se suscepto cum themate congruit Author"</note>
*It is fitting for one writing about the Cross to stand beneath the Cross.* <note>The author is likely referring to his imprisonment at Sonnenstein, suggesting that he is not just writing about suffering theoretically, but experiencing it as he writes.</note>
*If the Reader should perchance ask why he writes about the Cross?*
*He wishes to alleviate the Cross through his writings along with the Cross.*
*Christ alleviates it: He crowns the smallest and sweet crosses,*
*When we carry our crosses with a heart united to Him.*
*Hence the Cross received from the hand of the Lord, with a willing heart*
*Is borne as a sweet yoke and a light burden.* <note>This imagery draws from Matthew 11:30: "For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light."</note>

---

> As for me, God forbid that I should boast, except in the Cross of our Lord JESUS Christ, by which the world is crucified to me, and I to the world. Galatians VI. v. 14.
> 
> Whoever wants to come after me, let him renounce himself, and carry his Cross, and follow me. Matthew XVI. v. 24.

### VI.

The style of this little work will seem a bit unusual to you, I know it well; but it must be forgiven in light of the circumstances of the Author, who, after having suffered a confinement of more than eight months without paper, pen, or ink, finally obtained, after his release, this small comfort: to commit these thoughts on the <term>Mystery of the Cross</term> <note>The "Mystery of the Cross" refers to the central theme of the work: the spiritual necessity of suffering and the internal "crucifixion" of the self.</note> and others—with which he was as heavy as a pregnant woman—onto paper. Thus, to relieve and cheer his mind and heart a little, he made use of the style that first presented itself, without selection or refinement, these thoughts having flowed onto the paper of their own accord, without study and without much reflection; being the work of as many days as you will find chapters, and of only a few hours per day, as much as he...

<summary>The author describes the spontaneous and urgent nature of this work, which was written immediately following an eight-month imprisonment where he was denied writing materials. He explains that the text flowed out of him naturally, as if he were giving birth to ideas he had carried throughout his confinement.</summary>
<keywords>Theophilus, Mystery of the Cross, spiritual nothingness, prison writing, spontaneous composition, mysticism</keywords>

# NOTICE
## TO THE READER.

This is not the place, nor the time to recount every fact, nor the circumstances that gave occasion and birth to this little <term>Treatise</term> <note>original: "Traité." In this period, a "treatise" was a formal written work that systematically explored a specific spiritual or philosophical subject.</note>; this may well be done in the future, by a separate writing, if I recognize therein the will of the <term>Sovereign Master</term> <note>original: "souverain Maître." A title for God, emphasizing His absolute authority over the life of the believer.</note>, who calls and leads to Himself all His <term>creatures</term> <note>original: "créatures." This term refers to all created beings, specifically humans in their relationship to their Creator.</note> who are obedient to His voice, through <term>paths</term> <note>original: "sentiers." A common metaphor in mystical literature for the individual spiritual journey.</note> both sweet and harsh, smooth and rugged, sown with roses and thorns, according to His good pleasure and our need, and consequently impenetrable to reason and <term>human wisdom</term>, which is but foolish and blind in the <term>ways of God</term>.

<summary>In this preface, the author explains that the specific origins of the book remain a secret for now, attributing the work’s existence to the mysterious and often difficult guidance of God.</summary>
<keywords>preface, divine will, spiritual journey, human wisdom, providence, ways of God</keywords>

<header>Notice to the Reader</header>

## II.

Such <term>divine conduct</term> <note>original: "conduite divine." This refers to the way God actively directs and governs an individual's life through specific events and trials.</note> must be considered especially with the eyes of faith in the following writing of the *<term>Mystery of the Cross</term>* <note>original: "Mystère de la Croix." ## C H A P T E R IV.

### On the Foolishness of the Cross.

The wise men of the worldly School have made a small Deity out of their natural reason, which they, along with the Pagans <note>original: "Gentils"</note>, call a particle of the spirit, or of the divine light, *a small breath of divine air* <note>original: "divinæ particulam Auræ," a phrase from the Roman poet Horace suggesting that the human soul is a piece of the divine</note>. Within this beautiful perspective of their very limited vision, they have placed it like a Goddess upon the Altar of Truth, and have even introduced it into the Sanctuary itself, to judge and decide upon divine matters, or to explain and interpret them in its own way, recognizing no other light or guide in man except that one to arrive at the knowledge of the Truth. The three great branches <note>original: "partis," likely referring to the Catholic, Lutheran, and Reformed (Calvinist) confessions of the time</note> of Christianity have made, and still make, it their Idol; they consult it in their doubt, pronouncing its decisions with a proud arrogance as if they were divine oracles, and subjecting all other men—blindly led by the blind—to its laws and decrees. Since they have departed from the center of the Unity of divine truth, one must

### Chap. IV. On the Foolishness of the Cross.

VI. Indeed, is there anything more opposed to reason and human wisdom than to hate oneself, to take upon oneself contempt, poverty, infamy, and the lack of all things; to do good to those who do us harm; to love those who hate us; to pray for those who persecute us; to bless those who curse us; to die to our own will, to the pursuit and love of ourselves, of our comforts and pleasures; to choose everywhere the last place, the least delicate portions, and the least precious clothes: to leave Father, Mother, Brother, Sister, Wife, Children, Relatives and Friends, possessions and country—yes, to leave oneself—to submit to a vile, abject, contemptible, mortifying, and crucifying state? ## CHAPTER VII.

### On External Crosses.

Man's wounds are so desperately dangerous, and his ulcers so incurable (*Jeremiah 30:12*), that Eternal Wisdom <note>Eternal Wisdom (Sagesse éternelle) is a common personification of Christ or the Divine Mind, acting as a physician for the soul.</note> is forced to use iron and fire, and all manner of crosses and means, for his healing—or at least to awaken him from his deep lethargy, just as one uses blisters <term>Blisters (Vésicatoires): Medicated plasters applied to the skin to create a blister, historically used to "draw out" illness or stimulate a patient out of a coma or lethargy.</term> and the probe <term>The Probe (La sonde): A surgical tool used to explore the depth of a wound; here a metaphor for God examining the hidden depths of human sin.</term> in certain cases of disease and injury. IV. # CHAPTER VIII.

## On the Use of Crosses.

To make good use of a thing, one must know what it is in itself, where it comes from, what it is intended for, and where it leads. We have seen in several places what the Cross is in itself, and the marvelous mysteries it contains: All the little crosses of men are taken from the great Cross of JESUS, like so many particles of the Whole. They are sent, regulated, measured, and proportioned according to this great model by Divine Wisdom <note>In this context, Divine Wisdom refers to the providential planning of God, who "weighs" suffering to ensure it does not exceed a believer's strength.</note>, who shares and distributes them according to the need and capacity of each person.

# CHAPTER IX.

## *On the abuse of Crosses & especially that of JESUS.*

The natural man <note>In mystical theology, the "natural man" refers to a person living only by their physical senses and worldly reason, lacking spiritual rebirth or enlightenment.</note>, who understands nothing of divine things, also wants to hear nothing of the Cross, for which he feels only horror. When a cross happens to him—as it inevitably does—he becomes vexed, impatient, and murmurs; he blames the creatures <note>The "creatures" refers to created things or other people, rather than looking toward the divine cause or purpose of the suffering.</note>, whom he regards as the causes of his misfortunes. He grows pale and trembles with anger, like a stubborn beast that refuses to submit to the yoke being imposed upon it. 

Natural reason alone—which is that little spark of light <note>The "spark of light" (*scintilla animae*) is a common mystical term for the remnant of the divine image left in the human soul after the Fall.</note> remaining in man after his fall, and which leads the Schools to call him a rational animal <note>original Latin reference: *animal rationale*. This was the standard definition of humanity in Scholastic philosophy.</note>—should at least make him more docile in suffering the adversities that come upon him, so as not to make his burden heavier and not to become a burden to himself and others. Other spirits, who wish to be seen as "strong-minded" <note>The author likely refers here to the *esprits forts*, a term for the free-thinkers or skeptics of the 17th and 18th centuries who prided themselves on reason over faith.</note>, truly submit themselves to the ac—

<summary>This page begins Chapter IX, critiquing the "natural man" for his angry and impatient reaction to suffering (the Cross), arguing that even basic human reason should teach a person to bear burdens more gracefully.</summary>

# CHAPTER XIII.

## *Of the wonders of the Cross in external nature.*

The more external things distance themselves from unity, or from their center, the more they overflow into variety, multiplicity, and divisibility; whereas the central Point from which they emerged remains always constant, unique, and indivisibly united with itself, ceaselessly drawing the periphery toward itself: for the center constrains, and the circumference dilates. Thus, creatures, by moving away from their center, also move away from its power, its influence, and its irradiation <note>original: "irradiation" — in this context, the spiritual or physical light and energy that shines out from a divine or natural source.</note>: from which they become weaker, more powerless, and more contrary to one another, because of the diversity brought about by multiplicity. But it is nonetheless in this variety, caused by plurality, that the wonders of Unity appear, which would not be manifested at all without its own self-communication through plurality, in which we see shining forth the goodness, wisdom, and...

the People who all awaited Him as their Savior and the Restorer of the Kingdom of Israel, who consequently ought to have received Him, listened to Him, followed Him, loved Him, respected Him, and honored Him, being their brother according to the flesh and the liberator from their enemies according to the spirit. Here at last, my dear Theophilus <note>The name Theophilus means "friend of God" and was a common way for mystical or theological authors to address their readers, following the example of the Gospel of Luke.</note>, are my thoughts on the most profound mystery of the Cross, which you desired of me, and which the Lord has given me the grace and strength to treat in a manner that is perhaps very little known. From the heavenly realms <note>original: "Sedibus a superis"</note> down to the lowest shores descended
The Cross, blessed by Heaven <note>original: "Polo" — the celestial pole or the heavens</note>, yet cursed by the Earth <note>original: "Solo" — the soil or the ground</note>.

The Cross, the death of enemies and the salvation of mankind.
*Hail*, O Cross, vanquisher of the Underworld <note>original: "Erebus" — a term from Greek mythology for the dark region of the underworld, here used by the author to signify Hell</note>, triumphing over death!

Be broken, O bonds, and open wide, O barriers: O chains
Be loosened: your victor is here with the Cross.
The Cross ascends laden with spoils, decorated with trophies:

# CONCLUSION.

Here at last, my dear Theophilus <note>The name "Theophilus" means "Friend of God" or "Lover of God." While it could refer to a specific patron, it was commonly used in spiritual literature as a symbolic address to any devout reader seeking wisdom.</note>, are my thoughts on the most profound mystery of the Cross, which you requested of me, and which the Lord has granted me the grace and strength to address in a manner that is perhaps very little known. If there is anything good within, it comes from the inexhaustible fountain of life and light, without which we are but weakness and ignorance. Anything bad that might be found there certainly comes from me, and from an intellect <note>original: "raison" — referring here to the human capacity for logic and reasoning, which the author believes must be humbled before divine truth.</note> that is perhaps not yet sufficiently brought under the laws and the yoke of the Cross and of grace.

I could have made the volume larger, but readers are too easily put off by long-winded works that leave them no room to breathe. Moreover, much can be said in few words. If I have said but a few things with many words, I ask your indulgence for the state in which I find myself <note>The author hints at personal hardship, perhaps illness, old age, or the constraints of his current living situation, as an excuse for any stylistic failings.</note>; your boredom will soon pass, given the smallness of the volume.

As you may have found therein

A SACRED LITTLE GARDEN
<note>original Latin: "Hortulus Sacer"</note>

## II.

->*The Transmuting Stone.*<-
<note>original Latin: "Lapis transmutans" — A reference to the Philosopher's Stone of alchemy, which was believed to turn base metals into gold. Here, the author uses it as a metaphor for spiritual transformation through Christ or Divine Wisdom.</note>

To the *Stone of the Sun*, you lead me, Virgin Wisdom:
<note>original: "Lapis Solis" — The "Stone of the Sun" or the "Solar Stone," representing the highest achievement in alchemy (gold/perfection). "Sophia" is the Greek word for Wisdom, often personified in mystical literature.</note>
For in this way you are accustomed to play with your disciples:
Let others seek the Stone after the manner of the Sages:
<note>original: "Sophorum" — referring to the "Sophists" or alchemists who sought physical wealth or secret knowledge.</note>
To me, you are the Moon-making and Sun-making Stone.
<note>original: "Lunificus, Solificusque" — Neologisms meaning "making silver" (Moon) and "making gold" (Sun). Spiritually, this suggests the purification of both the soul and the spirit.</note>
The heavenly flesh is the Moon-maker; and the Blood of Wisdom
Is the Sun-making Stone: both white and red.
<note>The colors "white" (albedo) and "red" (rubedo) are the two final stages of the alchemical "Great Work." Here, the author links them to the bread and wine (flesh and blood) of the Eucharist.</note>
You change death into life: grief into joys;
Darkness into light: all evil into good:
And war into peace; you balance labor with rest,
And mourning with happiness. A wondrous Stone born from fire!

## III.

->*Christ Reborn.*<-
<note>original Latin: "Christus renascens"</note>

O Christ, I shall celebrate your glory, wonders, and praises:
And I shall honor the kind deeds of your power.

->IV.<-

### *The Dove to the Dove*
<note>original: "Columba ad Columbum." In mystical literature, the "dove" often represents both the human soul seeking God and the Holy Spirit or Christ responding. It is a symbol of purity and longing.</note>

Christ is the Father’s gentle heart, pure

Unconquered Love conquers himself; the free is bound:
The Victor is vanquished: life dies within him.
O cruel Love, too savage toward your very self!
Withhold from innocent blood! Punish the guilty.
To thoroughly wash away so many sins through a thousand
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;worlds,
A single tiny drop of blood is enough: spare
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;yourself.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;from everywhere, until
The entire company <note>The "company" (cohors) refers to the collective body of humanity.</note> is washed clean from every crime.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;deep!
<note>This echoes the dimensions of Christ's love described in Ephesians 3:18.</note>

You are full Light! Overflowing Salvation! Eternal
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;life!

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;heart!
O Lamb of God <note>original: "Agne Dei"</note> ever-dying, and perpetual
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;<term>offering</term>!
<note>The term "hostia" refers to a sacrificial victim or the consecrated bread of the Eucharist.</note>

Grant that in your death, my life may be an offering

Forever sacrificed to the eternal Father!
O Fountain! Open yourself to thirsty souls! We shall be satisfied:
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;in You
The whole salvation of men and all glory is revealed!

->Nothing is ours.<-

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;this and that!"

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;belongs to God?

## VII.

->The Sacred Kiss of Love. An Echo.<-
<note>original: "Sacrum Amoris osculum. Echo." This poem uses a Baroque literary device where the "Echo" repeats the final syllables of a phrase to create a new meaning, representing a dialogue between the Soul and God.</note>

*Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth. Song of Solomon 1:1.*
<note>original: "Cant. I. v. I." The Song of Solomon (Canticles) was historically interpreted as an allegory for the love between Christ and the Soul.</note>

What new voice strikes the breezes and our 
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;ears?
*Echo:* A sound. <note>original: "Res"</note> And what is this cry in our 
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;breast?
*Echo:* Love. <note>original: "Amor"</note>
Love, a friendly torturer, and great from a small 
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;origin.
*Echo:* The Lamb. <note>original: "Agnus"</note> Sweet melody! *Echo:* The mouth. <note>original: "Os"</note> From Love?
*Echo:* By custom. <note>original: "More"</note>
Break off delays. *Echo:* Do you pray? <note>original: "Oras?"</note> I pray to you with my whole 
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;heart. *Echo:* The heart. <note>original: "Cor."</note>
Will you not bless the heart devoted to You? *Echo:* Are you departing? <note>original: "Abis?"</note>
I am consumed by cares. *Echo:* You burn me. <note>original: "Uris."</note> I do not burn others, but I am burned 
By half-spoken words. *Echo:* Twice. <note>original: "Bis."</note> You play poorly, Love:
Nor do you answer well. *Echo:* You promise. <note>original: "Spondes."</note> I shall pledge my
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;faith. *Echo:* The same. <note>original: "Idem."</note>
Sacred faith! At last you take pity. *Echo:* You shall be. <note>original: "Eris."</note>

## VIII.

### Nothing perishes.
<note>original Latin: "Nihil perit"</note>

O wonder! From the burnt trunk of wood, Salt is produced:
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;From purified salt, a spiritual water.
Let the waters be cooked by fire, and the salt will be reborn 
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;from there:
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Which will provide medical aid to the sick.
An immortal power resides in salts! It is proven by 
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Art, <note>In this context, "Art" refers to Alchemy or Spagyrics—the early modern science of separating and recombining the essences of natural materials.</note>
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;That salts possess something of the hidden Deity.
The end of all things seems to be ash,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;But the end of ash is said to be glass. <note>The author refers to the process of vitrification, where plant ashes (potash) are melted at high heat to create glass, seen here as a "resurrection" of the plant's form.</note>
Art does this: what then cannot the Creator of Nature 
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;and Art do?
The earth gave this from what was cast aside: what will the 
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Stars give?

<note>The vocabulary at the bottom lists the central themes of the page: Sacred Garden, Salt, water, ash, glass, Deity, Art, Nature, Stars.</note>

<summary>This page concludes an allegorical dialogue of divine love and presents a poem on the "immortal power" of salts, arguing that if human alchemy can transform ash into glass, God can certainly grant eternal life. It reflects a mystical view of nature where even discarded matter contains a "hidden Deity."</summary>

# IX.

->*Love, the Restorer of all things.*<-
<note>original Latin: "Amor omnium Restitutor"</note>

To whom is greater virtue owed, greater glory,
To Christ, or the Serpent? Solve this: the conclusion
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;is clear.
If the Serpent was able to kill all things:
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Will the blood of Christ not be able to bring all things back to life?
Affection is stronger than hell: Love is stronger
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;than wrath: the eternal fountain <note>The Latin "latex" refers to a liquid or flowing water, here symbolizing the life-giving grace or blood of Christ.</note> is stronger than fire.
Light will overcome darkness and life will overcome death.
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Love will at last
Mortify all things, and Love will bring all things back to life.
<note>"Mortify" (mortificabit) here carries the spiritual sense of putting the "old self" or sin to death so that the soul can be reborn.</note>

# X.

->*On the same Restoration: The Lion and the Lamb.*<-
<note>original Latin: "De eadem Restitutione: Leo & Agnus"</note>

You who act, and teach us to spare our enemies,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;excusing their
Ignorance, and praying for their salvation: <note>A reference to Christ’s words on the cross: "Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do" (Luke 23:34).</note>
And you command us to bless those who curse:
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;will your
Wrath always rage against the hostile flock?
As a Lion you will indeed lead the hardy herds through fire
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;And through water, until they become soft
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;and pure.
<note>The poet suggests that God’s "wrath" is actually a form of "Lion-like" discipline—a refining process (fire and water) meant to purify the "hostile flock" rather than destroy them eternally.</note>

<term>Restitutor</term> (Restorer): One who returns things to their original, perfect state.
<term>Restitutio</term> (Restoration): The theological concept that all fallen beings will eventually be reconciled with God.
<term>Dilectio</term> (Affection/Love): A specific type of esteemed or choice-based love, often distinguished from purely emotional love.
<term>Gregem</term> (Flock): A common biblical metaphor for humanity or the Church.

<summary>This page presents two poems arguing for the ultimate triumph of divine love over death and wrath, asserting that Christ’s power to save must be greater than the Serpent’s power to destroy. It frames God’s discipline not as eternal punishment, but as a purifying process that leads all of creation back to a state of purity.</summary>

->*Winged Love. A Ship.*<-
<note>original: "Amor alatus. Navis." This emblem compares the soul's journey to God to both a bird in flight and a ship at sea.</note>

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;flight,

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;gain. <note>The author suggests that the "loss" of earthly attachments in the "fire" of devotion is actually a spiritual profit.</note>

*Eternity perceived, but not grasped.*

->in the depths<-

## XX.

### *Conscience speaks.*
<note>original: "Conscientia loquitur."</note>

As no one escapes themselves, so no one escapes me: I am for everyone the
    Tribunal <note>original: "Tribunal." In Roman law, this was the raised platform where a magistrate sat to administer justice.</note>
Attesting to the Throne of the eternal Divinity.
I point the way, and as a Witness I accuse you of guilt;
    I take on the roles of both the Judge and the Executioner. <note>original: "Carnificisque." A carnifex was a public official responsible for torture and execution; here, it personifies the "stings" of a guilty conscience.</note>
Often the avenger follows quickly on the heels of the guilty;
    But I pierce the inner depths, and count the very heartstrings, <note>original: "fibras," literally the fibers of the organs, used here to mean the most intimate parts of the soul.</note>

    crime is punished everywhere by its own penalty.

follows when I am the judge; when I strike, there is pain.
Consult me, weigh yourself by me: for I am the scale
    Attesting to the balance of the eternal Judge. <term>statera... libra</term> <note>The author uses two terms for weighing: "statera" (the physical scale) and "libra" (the balance or the weight itself), emphasizing the precision of divine judgment.</note>

## XXVII.
### *The Lily teaching mortals.*

O mortal man (*a*), you who come forth like a flower:
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;And like a flower, you wither in the decaying
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;field!
<note>Reference (*a*): Job 14:2. "He comes out like a flower and withers."</note>

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;This whiteness of mine is the honor
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;of chaste virginity.
<note>Reference (*b*): Matthew 6:29. "Even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these." The lily is a traditional symbol of the Virgin Mary and purity.</note>
I both live and die: but even so I rise again from death:
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Spring gives me life; cruel winter
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;slaughters me.

## XXVIII.

### Clemency.
<note>original: "Clementia." In this context, it refers to the virtue of mercy or leniency, specifically the restraint of power.</note>

To the beasts, a foreseeing cause gave little claws,

To the naked and fragile man, [Nature] gave the love of devotion,

More safely and better does she rule those whom Clemency subdues;
&nbsp;&nbsp;A heart without bitterness governs better than a hand without sweetness.

### XXIX.
#### *Justice speaking of herself.*
<note>original: "Justitia de se ipsa." In this poetic form, the virtue of Justice speaks directly to the reader to explain her purpose.</note>

Both the vine and vice grow too tall and wild
&nbsp;&nbsp;Unless they feel the pruning hand; I am the whetstone that tests them both.
Like a lightning bolt, I strike only a few, but I terrify many;
&nbsp;&nbsp;I correct most things with warnings, and many with threats.
By my hand, no one dies except him whose life was a cause for regret;
&nbsp;&nbsp;Through me, many things feel pain, which would be a tragedy to lose!
<note>Justice describes herself as a gardener who prunes "vice" to let the "vine" flourish. Her punishments are intended to be a deterrent to many, even if they only fall upon a few.</note>

## X X X.

### *Faustina’s devotion to her Father.*
<note>original: "Faustinae in Patrem pietas." This refers to the famous classical motif known as "Roman Charity" (*Caritas Romana*). In the traditional legend, the daughter is usually named Pero and her father Cimon, but here the author uses the name Faustina.</note>

Condemned to die, with hands and feet bound fast,
&nbsp;&nbsp;The old man was ordered to perish by a slow death.
For a long time, Faustina secretly preserved her captive Father
&nbsp;&nbsp;At her breast; she who was once a daughter was now a mother to him.
<note>The daughter breastfeeds her starving father to keep him alive in his cell, an act that traditionally symbolizes "Piety" or the ultimate fulfillment of duty to one's parents.</note>
The loyalty of the guards fell under suspicion; suspicion began
&nbsp;&nbsp;To fall upon the daughter’s trickery, or rather, the love of her devotion.
And so the shrewd Guard, when he saw the Father
&nbsp;&nbsp;Brought to the daughter’s breast, spoke thus in a rage:
"O, what a vain spirit! It is well known what a woman is capable of:
&nbsp;&nbsp;It is known that a woman is never devoted without some deceit."
<note>The guard views her act of mercy as a "fraud" because she bypassed the death sentence, reflecting the tension between man-made law and higher moral devotion.</note>

## X X X I.

### *Patience.*

Be a lamb: reflect the ways of the lamb; a lamb is gnawed
&nbsp;&nbsp;To its very bones in silence: press your lips tight while enduring.
<note>original: "Os, pariendo preme." The poet uses the metaphor of the lamb, which remains silent even when facing slaughter, to instruct the reader to endure suffering without complaint. The word "pariendo" (giving birth/bringing forth) suggests that this silence should be maintained even during the most intense "labor" of life's hardships.</note>

<summary>This page presents two moral lessons: the legend of a daughter breastfeeding her starving father to illustrate extreme filial devotion, and a metaphor of a silent lamb to encourage the virtue of patience during suffering.</summary>
<keywords>Faustina, Roman Charity, Caritas Romana, filial piety, devotion, patience, moral emblems, sacrifice, silence</keywords>

# XXXII.
## *Arise, you who sleep.*
<note>original: "Surge, qui dormis." A reference to Ephesians 5:14, calling for spiritual awakening.</note>

Immortal man! Why do you grow sluggish in a lazy life,
You who were born for eternity? From whence comes this so heavy
->slumber?<-
Arise: open your eyes: shake off the
->sleep<-
that weighs you down:
A violent force seizes the Kingdom of Heaven.
<note>The "violent force" refers to Matthew 11:12, suggesting that the kingdom of heaven requires earnest, forceful effort and spiritual vigor rather than passive laziness.</note>

# XXXIII.
## *Let it be.*
<note>original: "Fiat." This Latin term is used for both the creation of the world ("Let there be light") and Mary's acceptance of the incarnation.</note>

From every side, how great a power is made by the passive ***Word***!
->***Word***!<-
As both God himself creating, and Mary
->teach.<-
Out of nothing, the first (a) *Let it be* creates all things:
->*Let it be*<-
The second (b) brings forth God from the internal
->womb.<-
<note>original: "devehit orbe," literally "carries down from the sphere/circle," referring here to the womb or the earthly realm into which God is brought.</note>
So that the active *Word* may create from you all things
->which He wills:<-
Learn, by being silent, to endure as a passive
->*Let it be*.<-
<note>The author contrasts the "active" Word of God’s creation with the "passive" acceptance of Mary. The reader is encouraged to find strength in "suffering" or "enduring" (*pati*) in silence, echoing the earlier theme of the lamb.</note>

<summary>This page contains two meditative emblems: the first exhorts the reader to wake from spiritual lethargy to pursue heaven, and the second explores the theological significance of the word "Fiat" in creation and the Annunciation.</summary>

### XXXIV.

->*The opened side of Christ.*<-
<note>original: "Apertum Christi latus." This refers to the wound in Jesus' side inflicted by a lance during the Crucifixion.</note>

**Where corruption flows from the wound of fallen Adam:**
There flows equally the seen water of salvation.
<note>The poet contrasts the "sanies" (original: "sanies," meaning the discharge from a wound or moral corruption) of Adam's sin with the life-giving water that flowed from Christ's side.</note>

---

### XXXV.

->*Now the Kingdom is mixed, later it will be pure.*<-
<note>original: "Nunc Regnum mixtum, postea purum." This reflects the theological idea that the world currently contains both good and evil, which will only be separated at the end of time.</note>

Now the lilies bloom among thorns: the Kite
Ravages among the birds, and the Wolf among the sheep.
<note>The "Kite" (original: "Milvus") is a bird of prey, used here as a symbol of the wicked who persecute the innocent.</note>
**Fire will consume the thorns, and the Kite and the Wolf:**
And at the same time the Lilies, the birds, and the
sheep will rejoice.

---

### XXXVI.

->*O proud man! Why are you proud?*<-
<note>original: "O superbe! quid superbis?"</note>

**You who walk with a threatening face, full of yourself and anger:**
Despising all things with a puffed-up brow:
You were conceived as a fetus; but you were also born an infant, amidst
Dung and urine. From whence, O man, are you
proud?
<note>The author uses the "inter sterquilinium" trope—common in medieval and early modern devotional writing—reminding the reader of the lowly, physical reality of birth to combat spiritual pride.</note>

### XXXVII.

->*Empty Humility.*<-
<note>original: "Humilitas vacua." This refers to the spiritual state of being "empty" of ego or worldly pride so that one may be filled by grace.</note>

Just as the waves flow abundantly from the hills into the valley:
So God fills the empty and humble with love.

### XXXVIII.

->*Nothingness.*<-
<note>original: "Nihilum."</note>

Do you wish to become something? Remember first to be nothing:
Nothingness is the material out of which the Whole creates all things.
<note>The "Whole" (original: "Totum") is used here as a name for God, the Creator who brings the universe out of nothing (*ex nihilo*).</note>

### XXXIX.

->*The Silkworm.*<-
<note>original: "Bombix."</note>

->*A Symbol of Solitude and Resurrection.*<-

Covered in its own cocoon, the Silkworm weaves threads of pure silk,
In which man takes pride, though he has no right to do so.
<note>The poet notes the irony of human vanity: we dress in silk to feel superior, yet the silk is merely the product of a humble worm.</note>
Thus far from the crowds, enclosed within myself,
I usefully re-spin the threads of my life.
He who clothes the little worm with wings, even me—a worm—
God is able to transform, after my death.
<note>The silkworm was a popular "emblem" or moral symbol in the 17th century. Its transformation from a crawling larva to a winged moth within a cocoon served as a perfect metaphor for the Christian soul's retreat from the world and its eventual resurrection into a glorified body.</note>

## XL.

### *Slave and Freeman.*
<note>original: "Servus, Libertus." In Roman law, a *libertus* was a formerly enslaved person who had been legally freed (manumitted).</note>

When, though born free, I serve my sins, I am made
A slave! A heavy wrath holds me bound.
But when I, as a servant of Christ, devote myself to
Christ;
I become a Freeman: Love sets me free.
<note>The author plays on the legal term "manumission"—the formal act of a master freeing a slave. Here, Divine Love is the master who grants freedom.</note>

## XLI.

### *Praise, deceit, and the feminine.*
<note>original: "Laus, fraus, fœminina." This reflects a common, albeit harsh, 17th-century religious trope associating worldly temptation and vanity with traditional gender stereotypes.</note>

If you are wise, beware of crafty deceit and of praise:
Woman overflows with deceit; woman burns for
praise.

## XLII.

### Deadly Pleasure.
<note>original German: "Tödtliche Lust." This emblem shifts into the vernacular German to provide a rhyming moral aphorism.</note>

*In that which is only a burden to you, there God is not*
*lost:*
*In that which you now find pleasure, there Death is*
*born.*
<note>The poet suggests that spiritual "burdens" or suffering keep one close to God, whereas worldly "pleasure" (Lust) leads to spiritual death.</note>

## XLIII.

### *EVE and AVE.*
<note>original: "EVA, AVE." This refers to a famous medieval and Renaissance wordplay: "Eva" (the Latin name for Eve) is the reverse of "Ave" (the first word of the Angel Gabriel’s greeting to the Virgin Mary). It symbolizes the belief that Mary's obedience reversed the sin of Eve.</note>

EVE and AVE reveal, by the reversal of the name,
how it comes to pass...
<note>The text here is incomplete, likely continuing on the following page to explain the spiritual significance of this linguistic mirror.</note>

<summary>This page presents four moral emblems discussing the paradox of spiritual freedom through service to Christ, a warning against the vanity of praise, and the famous linguistic reversal of Eve's name (Eva/Ave).</summary>
<keywords>manumission, spiritual slavery, freedom in Christ, vanity, moral aphorisms, Eve and Mary, paradox, German poetry, Latin verse</keywords>

### XLIV.

#### *The Weavers of Spiders’ Webs.*
<note>original: "Aranearum telarum Textores."</note>

While the anxious spider toils over her fragile
->web:<-
Oh, how many companions does she have? You could
->hardly count them.<-
The learned and the unlearned! The great and the small: the
->powerful,<-
The weak: and those whom the Muse commands to be silent:
Men enriched by futile words and empty
->matters:<-
And those whom a vain self-assurance [plerophoria] rules.
<note>term: <term>plerophoria</term> is a Greek-derived word used in theology to mean "fullness of conviction." Here, the author uses it to describe a type of intellectual arrogance or dogmatic certainty.</note>
Those whom Criticism mocks, those whom the letter of the Word
->twists:<-
Those whom the Book and the Bottom
->occupy equally.<-
<note>The original Latin "Codex" (Book/Manuscript) and "Podex" (the rear/bottom) is a satirical rhyme. The author is mocking scholars who spend all their time sitting and reading, suggesting their intellectual work is as base as their physical functions.</note>

->subject<-
Divine laws to their own laws with rapid force.
<note>original: "Lapidis Sophici." This refers to alchemists who spent lifetimes trying to create the Philosopher's Stone, a legendary substance capable of turning lead into gold.</note>
And those whom the Squared Circle distresses
->by its turning:<-
And those whom a perpetual motion drives in a whirlwind.
<note>The "Squared Circle" (squaring the circle) and "perpetual motion" were the great "unsolvable" problems of the era. The author groups these scientific and mathematical obsessions with spiritual vanity, viewing them as fragile and useless "webs."</note>

### XLV.

### *The Idea of an Idea.*
<note>original: "Idea Ideae."</note>

The Idea is called the image of the soul and the idol of the
mind,
Giving birth to offspring, and bringing its own to life.
From this, one is called the "formed"; the other is called the
"former":
And thus she is a daughter to herself, and her own parent.
Yet both are chaste little maidens, pleasant, delicate,
Bright: a gentle image of the thing conceived.
Who could grasp the mother and the birth of this
Magic?
Unless the Idea paints its own mirror for the mind.
A single Idea of itself depicts a bright Idea:
For it brings itself forth, and makes Echo a Goddess.
<note>This poem personifies the philosophical concept of an "Idea." In the logic of the time, an idea was seen as a mental "simulacrum" (image) that reproduces itself in the mind like a reflection in a mirror or an echo of a voice.</note>

<summary>This page concludes a satire on social and intellectual vanity before introducing a philosophical poem on the self-generating nature of human thought and "Ideas."</summary>

### XLVI.

->*Eternity is a Point.*<-
<note>original: "Æternitas est Punctum."</note>

Though you count time as long-lived through the ages,
That which you can count is not eternal.
But a point, always self-sufficient, present, and indivisible—
<note>The author uses the word "infectile," meaning something that cannot be divided or "cut" into parts, referring to the mathematical definition of a point.</note>
That is eternal, for you are unable to count it.
<note>In the philosophy of this period, eternity was often envisioned not as a very long time, but as a "standing now" (*nunc stans*)—a single point that has no beginning, end, or duration that can be measured.</note>

### XLVII.

->*Finally an end, never an end.*<-
<note>original: "Tandem finis, nunquam finis."</note>

Those things to which time gave birth, cease with time:
Grief, struggle, anguish, death, pain, anger, and fury.
For the Abyss, which swallows both the beginning and the end,
<note>original: "Abyssus." In mystical theology, the "Abyss" often refers to the infinite nature of the Divine which exists outside of created time.</note>
Devours such monsters of fallen nature.
<note>original: "Natura lapsa." A theological term referring to the state of humanity and the world after the "Fall" from Eden, which introduced suffering and death.</note>
But that which flowed from an eternal origin
Never ceases: life shall be unceasing, and love everlasting.

<note>Vocabulary used on this page: Eternity (Æternitas), Point (Punctum), Abyss (Abyssus), Fallen Nature (Natura lapsa), life (vita), love (amor), time (tempus), end (finis).</note>

<summary>This page presents two short meditative poems defining eternity as an indivisible "now" rather than a long duration, and contrasting the temporary nature of human suffering with the eternal nature of divine life and love.</summary>
<keywords>eternity, metaphysics, the Abyss, fallen nature, time vs. eternity, suffering, divine love</keywords>

### XLVIII.

->*The radiant and ruddy Groom.*<-
<note>original: "Sponsus candidus & rubicundus." A reference to the Song of Solomon 5:10, traditionally interpreted in Christian mysticism as a description of Christ: "white" in his purity or divinity, and "ruddy" (red) in his humanity or his sacrifice on the cross.</note>

### XLIX.

->*Absalom hanging.*<-
<note>original: "Absálon pendulus." Refers to the biblical story of Absalom, the son of King David, who rebelled against his father.</note>

### L.

->*The Author's Triple Cross.*<-
<note>original: "Crux trina Authoris." A "cross" here is used metaphorically to mean a heavy burden or a period of suffering.</note>

The first cross was once imposed by a blind

### LI.

->*The Grand Climacteric Year 63.*<-
<note>original: "Annus Clymactericus magnus 63." In early modern medicine and astrology, the 63rd year of life (7 x 9) was known as the "Grand Climacteric," believed to be a critical turning point where one was most at risk of death or major life changes.</note>

This age denotes, as it is said, a thousand
perils:
And it portends many evils, and nothing
of good.
The poet who records these things has reached such an year:
In which my Freedom, my name, and my honor
perish.
Yet this year promises many gifts to me at the same
time:
In which my Freedom, my name, and my honor
return.
And at once the lying calumny of the common folk
falls silent:
And the rest feel regret and shame for what was
done.
But hope suggests another, more fortunate omen
to me;
Which *Wisdom* forbids me to speak with my
own voice.
<note>original: "Sophia." The author personifies Wisdom, suggesting a mystical or secret insight into his future that he cannot yet reveal.</note>

### LII.

->*The corruption of one is the generation of another.*<-
<note>original: "Unius corruptio, alterius generatio." A fundamental principle of Aristotelian natural philosophy, meaning that in the natural world, the decay of one thing is the necessary starting point for the birth of something else.</note>

### L I V.

# ELEGY

### On the Subject and Author of this book.

From here, far away! From the sacred sanctuaries, far 
    away, go, you uninitiated! <note>original: "procul ite, profani." This is a classical formula used in ancient Roman religion to warn the spiritually "unclean" to stay away from sacred rites. The author adopts this high-style tone to signal the sanctity of the text.</note>
  Here the *Initiate* <term>Initiate (Latin: Myſta): Derived from the Greek term for someone initiated into sacred mysteries. Here, it refers to the author as a mystical guide who reveals the hidden truths of the Cross.</term> bears the secrets of God and the Cross.
He bears sacred mysteries, not to be looked upon by the 
    wicked crowd,
He bears sacred mysteries, which are ever to be 
    revealed to the faithful.
You indeed, whose spirit is a breath 
    of divine light, 
  And whose Virtue is not an enemy to the Cross,
Draw near to these sacred rites; favor them with your heart and 
    tongues, <note>original: "animo linguisque favete." A ritual call for "holy silence" and reverent attention, typical of a priest beginning a ceremony.</note>
<margin>Chapter I.</margin> And, fastened to the Cross, learn to bear the 
    yoke.
Behold the secret roots of this tree, 
  and the origin from which the life-giving 
    Cross is established.
<margin>II. III.</margin> Learn what remedies come from this stem, 
  even more life-giving than those of Paradise: <note>The author argues that the wood of the Cross is more potent and restorative than the Tree of Life in the Garden of Eden.</note>
How much they avail the shoulders of those who do not 
    refuse to carry it;

->Hail, penalty of death, origin of a better birth,<-

How badly are they deceived, to whose back you are believed

O light and sweet burden! O lovable weight! Pressed
